Country primarily in Western Europe (pop., 2026: over 69.1 million), officially the French Republic. Its overseas regions and territories include French Guiana in South America, Saint Pierre and Miquelon in the North Atlantic, the French West Indies, and many islands in Oceania and the Indian Ocean. Its 18 integral regions, five of them overseas, cover 632,702 km². [[Paris]], the largest city, is the main cultural and economic center, with a metropolitan population of over 13 million.

Celtic tribes known as [[Gaul|Gauls]] settled the territory in the Iron Age, and Rome annexed it in 51 BC. The [[Franks]] formed the kingdom of Francia, heartland of the Carolingian Empire; the Treaty of Verdun of 843 partitioned that empire, and West Francia evolved into the Kingdom of France. The kingdom fought England in the [[Hundred Years' War]] from the mid-14th to the mid-15th century and, under [[Louis XIV]], built Europe's strongest army. The [[French Revolution]] of 1789 overthrew the ancien régime. [[Napoleon]] Bonaparte established the First French Empire, bringing France to its political and military zenith in the early 19th century. The Second Empire collapsed in the Franco-Prussian War in 1870, and the Third Republic followed. France emerged victorious from World War I at great human and economic cost, was occupied by Germany in 1940, and was liberated in 1944. The Fourth Republic dissolved over the course of the Algerian War, and the Fifth Republic, a semi-presidential system, was formed in 1958 by [[Charles de Gaulle]]. Algeria and most French colonies became independent in the 1960s.

France has 54 UNESCO World Heritage Sites, the fourth-largest number, and received 58 million foreign visitors in 2025. A developed country, it is a permanent member of the UN Security Council and an official nuclear-weapon state.

Capacity of agents to choose between possible courses of action, to exercise the control over their actions that moral responsibility requires, or to be the ultimate source of those actions. The central debate concerns whether and how such freedom can coexist with physical determinism, divine foreknowledge, and other constraints. Free will is closely linked to moral responsibility, praise, blame, and deliberation, since traditionally only freely willed actions are seen as deserving credit or blame.

The problem was identified in ancient Greek literature. A compatibilist notion of free will has been attributed to [[Aristotle]] and to Epictetus; according to Susanne Bobzien, an incompatibilist notion appears first in the works of Alexander of Aphrodisias in the 3rd century AD. The term *liberum arbitrium* was introduced by Christian philosophy in the 4th century AD and meant a lack of necessity in the human will.

[[Determinism]] holds that the natural world is governed by cause and effect, so that only one course of events is possible. Incompatibilists regard free will as inconsistent with it. Metaphysical libertarians argue that determinism is false and free will therefore possible; hard determinists argue that determinism is true and free will therefore impossible. Hard incompatibilists, or illusionists, hold that indeterminism is equally incompatible with free will.

Compatibilists hold that free will can coexist with determinism, though they define it differently. Classical compatibilists treated it as freedom of action: a person is free if, had they wanted to do otherwise, they could have done so without physical impediment. Many contemporary compatibilists treat it as a psychological capacity to direct one's behavior in a way that is responsive to reason.

Period of political and social upheaval in France (1789–99) that overthrew the monarchy and ended with Napoleon Bonaparte as First Consul. Many of its ideas are considered fundamental principles of liberal democracy, and its values remain central to French political discourse.

The revolution resulted from social, economic, financial, and political crises that the regime could not manage. Between 1715 and 1789 the population grew from 21 to 28 million, but living standards fell for wage laborers and tenant farmers. Economic recession from 1785 and bad harvests in 1787 and 1788 brought high unemployment and food prices. By 1788 half of state revenue went on servicing debt. Reform was blocked by the regional parlements, and [[Louis XVI]] often backed down before conservative opposition in the nobility. The [[American Revolution]] and Enlightenment critiques shaped public debate.

The crisis led to the convocation of the Estates General in May 1789, its first meeting since 1614. The Third Estate re-constituted itself as a National Assembly in June. The [[Storming of the Bastille]] on July 14 was followed by radical measures, including the abolition of feudalism, state control over the Catholic Church, and the [[Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen]].

The king's attempted flight to Varennes in June 1791 discredited the monarchy further. Military defeats after the outbreak of the [[French Revolutionary Wars]] in April 1792 led to the insurrection of August 10, 1792. The French First Republic replaced the monarchy in September, and Louis XVI was executed in January 1793. Power then passed to the Committee of Public Safety, dominated by Jacobins led by [[Maximilien Robespierre]]. About 16,000 people were sentenced by the Revolutionary Tribunal and executed in the [[Reign of Terror]], which ended in July 1794. The Directory took over in November 1795, and the coup of 18 Brumaire on November 9, 1799, established the Consulate under [[Napoleon]].

Romance language of the Indo-European family, spoken natively in France and in parts of Canada, Belgium, Switzerland, Luxembourg, and Monaco. French and its closest relatives, the langues d'oïl, historically spoken in northern France and southern Belgium, descended from the Vulgar Latin of the [[Roman Empire]]. Celtic languages of northern Roman Gaul and the Germanic Frankish language of the post-Roman invaders influenced it, and it largely supplanted regional [[Romance languages|Romance]] varieties across France, Belgium, and Switzerland.

Latin was gradually adopted in Gaul under Roman rule, and the local variety evolved into the Gallo-Romance tongues. Gaulish likely survived into the 6th century and left loanwords and calques, including *oui*, "yes"; the *Petit Robert* attributes 154 French words to it. Writing in Gaulish all but disappeared between the 4th and 5th centuries. The Ordinance of Villers-Cotterêts of 1539 mandated French in legal documents, and the Académie Française was established in 1635.

French is estimated to have about 310 million speakers, about 74 million of them native. It is the 22nd most natively spoken language, the sixth most spoken by total number of speakers, and among the five most studied, with about 120 million learners in 2017. It is an official language in 26 countries, and 54 states belong to the Organisation internationale de la Francophonie. In 2025 approximately 50% of the Francophone population lived in sub-Saharan Africa and the Indian Ocean, 30% in Europe, 15% in North Africa, and 7% in the Americas. Colonialism carried the language to the Americas, Africa, and Asia, and French-based creole languages developed, most notably Haitian Creole.

French has a long history as an international language of literature, diplomacy, and science. It is a primary or second language of many organizations, including the [[United Nations]], the [[European Union]], NATO, and the International Olympic Committee, and it is the second most widely spoken mother tongue in the European Union.

Relationship of mutual affection between people, stronger than an acquaintance or association such as that with a classmate, neighbor, or coworker. Common features include choosing to be with one another, enjoying time together, and offering positive support. Friends are sometimes distinguished from family and from lovers, though the line can blur.

Friendship is studied in communication, [[Sociology|sociology]], social psychology, anthropology, and philosophy. Proposed theories include social exchange theory, equity theory, relational dialectics, and attachment styles. A classification originating in classical philosophy distinguishes friendships based on utility, pleasure, and virtue. Research links high-quality friendships to reduced risk of depression, and evolutionary accounts describe friendship as an adaptation that secured non-kin alliances for cooperation and protection.

Children's understanding of friendship focuses on common activities, physical proximity, and shared expectations; friendships give them opportunities for play and practicing self-regulation. Based on reports from teachers and mothers, 75% of preschool children had at least one friend, a figure that rose to 78% through the fifth grade, when 55% had a mutual best friend. About 15% of children were chronically friendless, reporting periods of at least six months without mutual friends.

In [[Adolescence|adolescence]], friendships become more giving, sharing, frank, supportive, and spontaneous, and rest more on similar morals and values, loyalty, and shared interests. A large study of American adolescents found that those who engaged less in problematic behavior had friends who did well in school, took part in school activities, avoided drinking, and had good mental health.

In adulthood, friendship provides companionship, affection, and emotional support and contributes to mental and physical health. Workplace friendships can be hard to maintain. A 2023 Pew Research Center survey reported that 8% of respondents had no close friends and a further 7% had only one.

Seed-bearing structure of [[Flowering plant|flowering plants]] (angiosperms), formed from the ovary after flowering. Fruits are the means by which angiosperms disperse their seeds. Edible fruits propagate through the movements of humans and other animals, in a symbiosis that supplies the animals with nutrition, and they account for a substantial fraction of the world's agricultural output. Some, such as the [[Apple|apple]] and the pomegranate, have acquired extensive cultural and symbolic meanings.

Botanical and culinary usage differ. In botany, a fruit is a ripened ovary or carpel that contains seeds, as in the orange, pomegranate, [[Tomato|tomato]], and pumpkin; a nut is a type of fruit, not a seed, and a seed is a ripened ovule. In culinary language, a fruit is the sweet or sour produce of a specific plant, such as a peach, pear, or lemon, whereas vegetables are typically savory. Cucumbers, squashes, beans, peanuts, peas, corn, eggplants, and bell peppers are botanical fruits usually called [[Vegetable|vegetables]]. Many spices, including black pepper, chili pepper, cumin, and allspice, are also fruits. Rhubarb, often treated as a fruit in pies, is in fact the leaf stalk of the plant. A cereal grain such as rice or wheat is a fruit termed a caryopsis, but its wall is thin and fused to the seed coat, so the edible part is almost entirely seed.

The outer layer of most fruits is the pericarp, typically formed from the ovary and divisible into the epicarp, mesocarp, and endocarp. [[Pollination]] moves pollen to the stigma, and a pollen tube grows down the style to the ovule. One sperm unites with the egg to form a zygote, which gives rise to the embryo, and the other enters the central cell and gives rise to endosperm, a nutritive tissue; this is double fertilization. The ovules become seeds, while the pericarp may become fleshy, as in berries, or hard, as in nuts. Fruits to which other floral parts contribute significantly, such as the apple, strawberry, and pineapple, are called accessory fruits.

Rule assigning to each element of one set exactly one element of another set. A function from a set X to a set Y assigns to each element of X exactly one element of Y; X is called the domain and Y the codomain. If the function f assigns y to x, one says that f maps x to y and writes y = f(x). The set of values actually taken is the image, sometimes called the range, a subset of the codomain. A function is often defined by an expression such as f(x) = x² + 1, for which evaluation gives f(4) = 17.

Functions began as an idealization of how one varying quantity depends on another, as the position of a planet depends on time. The concept was elaborated with the infinitesimal [[Calculus|calculus]] at the end of the 17th century. [[Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz|Leibniz]] introduced the word "function" in 1673, and [[Leonhard Euler|Euler]] defined functions as analytic expressions in his *Introductio in analysin infinitorum* in 1748. Until the 19th century the functions considered were differentiable. At the end of the 19th century the concept was formalized in terms of [[Set theory|set theory]], which greatly widened its applications.

In the set-theoretic definition, a function is a binary relation between X and Y in which every element of X is related to exactly one element of Y. The set of all pairs (x, f(x)) is the graph of the function. When both sets are sets of [[Real number|real numbers]], each pair can be read as the Cartesian coordinates of a point in the plane. A function whose domain is a proper subset of X is called a partial function.

Important properties include injectivity (distinct inputs give distinct outputs), surjectivity (every element of the codomain is an output), and bijectivity (both, which allows an inverse). Functions are widely used in science, engineering, and most fields of mathematics, and have been called "the central objects of investigation" in most of them.

Member of a group of eukaryotic organisms, including yeasts, molds, and mushrooms, classified in the biological kingdom Fungi. Fungi differ from plants, bacteria, and some protists in having [[Chitin|chitin]] in their cell walls. Like animals, they are heterotrophs, absorbing dissolved organic molecules, typically by secreting digestive enzymes into their environment. They do not perform [[Photosynthesis|photosynthesis]]. The study of fungi is called [[Mycology|mycology]]; once regarded as a branch of botany, it is now known that fungi are genetically more closely related to animals than to plants.

The vegetative body of most fungi is a network of threads called [[Hypha|hyphae]], which together form the mycelium. Fungi reproduce both asexually and sexually, with [[Spore|spores]] as the main dispersal units. Most are inconspicuous, living in soil or on dead matter, and become noticeable when they fruit as mushrooms or molds. They are the principal decomposers in ecological systems and have fundamental roles in nutrient cycling. Most plants depend on mycorrhizal symbiosis with fungi.

Fungi have long served as food, as in mushrooms and truffles, as a leavening agent for bread, and in the fermentation of wine, beer, and soy sauce. Since the 1940s they have been used to produce antibiotics, and fungal enzymes are used industrially. Some species produce mycotoxins that are toxic to animals. Fungi can break down manufactured materials, and crop losses to fungal disease, such as rice blast, affect food supplies. Over 8,000 species are known to be detrimental to plants and at least 300 can be pathogenic to humans.

The kingdom ranges from unicellular aquatic chytrids to large mushrooms, and its diversity is estimated at 2.2 million to 3.8 million species, of which only a small fraction have been described. Fungi were classified by morphology from the pioneering work of Carl Linnaeus, Christiaan Hendrik Persoon, and Elias Magnus Fries; DNA analysis has since reshaped the groupings. The kingdom is divided into one subkingdom, seven phyla, and ten subphyla.

Objects intended to support human activities such as seating, eating, storing items, working, and sleeping. Stools, chairs, sofas, tables, desks, beds, cupboards, shelves, and drawers are all furniture. It can be made from many materials, including metal, plastic, and wood, using woodworking joints that often reflect local culture. Furniture can be a product of design and a form of decorative art, and it may serve a symbolic or religious purpose. The English word derives from French *fourniture*, from *fournir*, "to supply"; French and other Romance languages and German instead use variants of *meubles*, from Latin *mobilia*, "moveable goods".

People have used tree stumps, rocks, and moss as furniture since the beginning of human civilization. From around 30,000 years ago, people began to construct and carve furniture from wood, stone, and animal bones. A seated figure from [[Çatalhöyük]] in Turkey dates to between 6000 and 5500 BC. The houses of Skara Brae, a Neolithic village in Orkney, Scotland, dated 3100 to 2500 BC, contain the earliest surviving furniture: cupboards, dressers, beds, shelves, and seats built of stone because wood was scarce.

Complex construction techniques such as joinery began in the early dynastic period of [[Ancient Egypt]], which saw wooden stools and tables sometimes decorated with valuable metals or ivory. In [[Ancient Greece]] and [[Ancient Rome]], thrones were commonplace, as were the *klinai*, multipurpose couches for relaxing, eating, and sleeping.

Furniture of the [[Middle Ages]] was usually heavy, oak, and ornamented. Design expanded during the Italian [[Renaissance]] of the 14th and 15th centuries, and the 17th century was marked by opulent, often gilded [[Baroque]] designs. The 19th century is usually defined by revival styles, and the first three quarters of the 20th century are often seen as a march toward [[Modernism]].

System of stars, planetary systems, stellar remnants, interstellar gas, dust, and [[Dark matter|dark matter]] bound together by gravity. The word derives from the Greek *galaxias*, "milky", a reference to the [[Milky Way]], the galaxy that contains the Solar System. Galaxies average an estimated 100 million stars, ranging from dwarfs with fewer than a thousand stars to supergiants with one hundred trillion. Most of a typical galaxy's mass is dark matter, with only a few percent visible as stars and nebulae. [[Supermassive black hole|Supermassive black holes]] are a common feature at their centers.

Galaxies are categorized by their visual characteristics as elliptical, spiral, or irregular; the Milky Way is a spiral. An estimated 200 billion (2×10¹¹) to 2 trillion galaxies exist in the [[Observable universe|observable universe]]. Most are 1,000 to 100,000 parsecs in diameter (approximately 3,000 to 300,000 light-years) and are separated by millions of parsecs. The Milky Way has a diameter of at least 26,800 parsecs (87,400 light-years), and its nearest large neighbor, the [[Andromeda Galaxy]], is just over 750,000 parsecs (2.4 million light-years) away.

Most galaxies are gravitationally organized into groups, clusters, and superclusters. The Milky Way and Andromeda dominate the [[Local Group]], which is part of the [[Virgo Supercluster]]. At the largest scale these associations form sheets and filaments surrounded by immense voids. Galaxy formation is less well understood than star formation and operates on a scale of a billion years.

The Greek philosopher Democritus proposed that the Milky Way might consist of distant stars, while Aristotle attributed it to the ignition of exhalations in the upper atmosphere. Galaxies were first known telescopically as spiral nebulae and were called island universes once their distance beyond the Milky Way was recognized. [[Edwin Hubble]] kept to the term nebulae, and the nomenclature did not fully change until after his death in 1953.
